newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Kia car assembly in Russia to start in early 1997.
newsitem.headline: Kia car assembly in Russia to start in early 1997.

text.p: A Russian company will start assembling vehicles from Korean automaker Kia Motors Corp in early 1997 in a project planned to top $1 billion, Kia's sales office in Moscow told Reuters on Wednesday.

"Assembly will start in early 1997 -- no later than February," Denis Titov, a sales executive in the Moscow office of Korean conglomerate LG International Corp (LGI), which imports and distributes Kia vehicles in Russia and Ukraine.

The Russian company, privately-owned ZAO Avtotor, will launch operations in the Baltic port of Kaliningrad, Titov said. Production lines come from an idled car factory once used by Japanese automaker Nissan Motor Co Ltd in Greece, he said.
"Everything should arrive in Russia sometime in December," Titov said.
Initial output will include one or two Kia models -- probably Avella hatchbacks or Sephia sedans, Maxim Litvin, a senior sales executive for LGI in Moscow, told Reuters.

"A broader range of vehicles could be assembled in the future -- once output hits big volumes," he said. Other possible models include Besta vans, Clarus sedans, Pride hatchbacks and Sportage off-road vehicles.
Avtotor will assemble the vehicles from kits exported from Korea by Kia, Litvin said. Output could reach as many as 20,000 units in 1997 and 80,000 units in 1998, he added.
The vehicles will be exported throughout eastern Europe, but LGI could sell roughly 80 percent of the volumes in Russia, Titov said.

"We could sell almost all of the cars in Russia without a problem," he said. "The demand for mid-sized cars like Kias will be quite high next year, and the prices that we could offer on locally-produced cars would give us a great advantage."

Russia's taxes on imports of completely-built cars range from 65 percent to 95 percent, but cars assembled in Kaliningrad are exempt from duties because the Russian enclave is a tax-free zone, Litvin said.
"Prices on models assembled in Kaliningrad should fall as much as 35 percent from the current levels," Titov said. "This market is extremely price sensitive -- every thousand dollars counts."
LGI sold nearly 500 Kia vehicles in 1995, its first full year representing the automaker in Russia, Titov said. Sales should top 4,000 units in 1996, he added.
The Avtotor-Kia project is the latest in a series of major automotive investments in former communist Europe announced by Korean conglomerates in the mid-1990s.
Daewoo Group has been the most visible player with plans to invest over $3 billion to build vehicles in the Czech Republic, Poland, Romania, Russia and Uzbekistan.

Kia will not contribute significantly to the $1 billion planned for the Kaliningrad project, Litvin said. The investment will accumulate over the next 10 years mainly from Russian companies locating facilities there to supply accessories and parts for Kia assembly, he added.
